title: Bob Newhart
wiki_lead:
George Robert Newhart (September 5, 1929 – July 18, 2024) was an American comedian and actor. Newhart was known for his deadpan and stammering delivery style. Beginning his career as a stand-up comedian, he transitioned his career to acting in television. He received three Grammy Awards, an Emmy Award, a Golden Globe Award, a Peabody Award, a Hollywood Walk of Fame Star, and the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor.
Newhart came to prominence in 1960 when his record album of comedic monologues, The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart, became a bestseller and reached number one on the Billboard pop album chart and won two Grammy Awards for Album of the Year, and Best New Artist. That same year he released his follow-up album, The Button-Down Mind Strikes Back! (1960), which was also a success, and the two albums held the Billboard number one and number two spots simultaneously. He later released several additional comedy albums.
Newhart hosted a short-lived NBC variety show, The Bob Newhart Show (1961), before starring as Chicago psychologist Robert Hartley on The Bob Newhart Show from 1972 to 1978. For the latter, he won the Golden Globe Award for Best Male TV Star. He then starred as Vermont innkeeper Dick Loudon on the series Newhart from 1982 to 1990, where he received three nominations for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series. He also starred in two short-lived sitcoms, Bob (1992–1993) and George and Leo (1997–1998).
Newhart also acted in the films Hell Is for Heroes (1962), Hot Millions (1968), Catch-22 (1970), Cold Turkey (1971), In & Out (1997), and Elf (2003), and voiced Bernard in the Disney animated film The Rescuers (1977) and its sequel (1990). Newhart played Professor Proton on the CBS sitcom The Big Bang Theory from 2013 to 2018, for which he received his first-ever career Emmy Award, for the Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series. He also reprised his role in The Big Bang Theory prequel spin-off series Young Sheldon (2017–2020).

Early life and education
George Robert Newhart was born on September 5, 1929, in Oak Park, Illinois. His parents were Julia Pauline (née Burns; 1901–1994), a housewife, and George David Newhart (1899–1987), a part-owner of a plumbing supply business. His mother was of Irish descent, while his father was of German and Irish descent. He went by his middle name, "Bob," to avoid confusion with his father. The family name Newhart is of German origin (Neuhart). One of his grandmothers was from St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada. He had three sisters.
Newhart was educated at Catholic schools in the Chicago area, including St. Catherine of Siena Grammar School in Oak Park, and attended St. Ignatius College Prep (high school), graduating in 1947. He then enrolled at Loyola University Chicago, from which he graduated in 1952 with a bachelor's degree in business management. grok_lead: Bob Newhart (born George Robert Newhart; September 5, 1929 â July 18, 2024) was an American stand-up comedian and actor renowned for his deadpan, stammering comedic style that emphasized one-sided telephone conversations and everyman characters. He rose to fame in the early 1960s with groundbreaking comedy albums that topped the Billboard charts and earned him multiple Grammy Awards, before becoming a television icon through two long-running sitcoms that showcased his subtle humor and relatable persona. Newhart was born in Oak Park, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, to a middle-class Catholic family, the second of four children; his father co-owned a plumbing business, and his mother was a homemaker. After attending Roman Catholic schools and graduating from Loyola University Chicago in 1952 with a degree in business management, he briefly studied law before serving two years in the U.S. Army during the Korean War era and then working as an accountant in Chicago. His entry into comedy began in the late 1950s when, alongside friend Ed Gallagher, he recorded improvised routines on a home tape recorder, which caught the attention of a Chicago DJ and led to a Warner Bros. Records contract. Newhart's breakthrough came with his debut album, The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart (1960), which became the first comedy album to reach No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart and won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 1961, a feat unprecedented for a non-music release. Its follow-up, The Button-Down Mind Strikes Back! (1960), also topped the charts and secured another Grammy for Best Comedy Performance, establishing his signature style of understated, observational humor that influenced generations of comedians including Jerry Seinfeld and Bill Cosby. Transitioning to television, he hosted a short-lived variety show in 1961 before starring as psychologist Bob Hartley in The Bob Newhart Show (1972â1978), a CBS sitcom that ran for six seasons and earned multiple Emmy nominations for its ensemble cast and witty writing. His second major series, Newhart (1982â1990), cast him as innkeeper Dick Loudon in a rural Vermont setting, becoming another critical and commercial success with eight seasons on CBS and a memorable series finale in 1990 that revealed the entire run as a dream of his character from the earlier show. Newhart appeared in films such as Hell Is for Heroes (1962), Catch-22 (1970), and Elf (2003), where he played the pragmatic Papa Elf, and provided voice work for Disney's The Rescuers (1977) and its sequel. Later in his career, he earned an Emmy Award in 2013 for his recurring role as Professor Proton on The Big Bang Theory, and received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 2002 for his lifetime contributions to comedy. On a personal note, Newhart married Virginia "Ginnie" Quinn in 1963, and the couple remained together until her death in 2023 after 60 years; they had four childrenâRobert, Timothy, Courtney, and Jenniferâand ten grandchildren. In 1985, he was diagnosed with secondary polycythemia, a blood disorder caused by heavy smoking, but recovered after quitting smoking, and continued working into his later years, including stand-up tours and guest appearances. Newhart died at his home in Los Angeles at age 94 following a series of short illnesses, leaving a legacy as one of the most influential and beloved figures in American comedy.
